card.title: Describe a teacher who has influenced you.
points: what subject he or she taught you
what he or she was like
card.explain: and explain how this teacher has influenced you.

items.model:
I’d like to talk about my physics teacher in secondary school, Mr Saleh. He taught me for two years, when I was about sixteen and seventeen, and to be honest, he’s probably the main reason I decided to study engineering.

Before I was in his class, I found physics really dry. It was just a lot of formulas that I memorised for exams and then forgot. But Mr Saleh had a completely different approach. He always started his lessons with a real-life question, like why a car needs to slow down before a bend, or how a plane manages to stay in the air. Then he would show us how the formulas actually answered those questions. Suddenly the subject made sense.

He was also incredibly patient. If someone didn’t understand, he would explain it again in a different way, and he never made anyone feel stupid for asking. And he had a great sense of humour, so his classes were never boring.

As for how he influenced me, I think the biggest thing was that he believed in me. At one point I was struggling with my grades, and he stayed after school a few times to help me catch up. He told me I had a talent for problem-solving and encouraged me to consider engineering. That gave me a lot of confidence. Even now, when I face a difficult problem, I try to do what he taught us: break it down into smaller questions and start with the simplest one.

p3.q: What qualities make a good teacher?
p3.model: I’d say patience is essential, because students learn at different speeds. A good teacher also needs to make the subject relevant, so students understand why it matters. And finally, I think they should be fair and treat every student with respect, which encourages students to participate.

p3.q: Will technology replace teachers in the future?
p3.model: I don’t think so, at least not completely. Technology is great for practising skills and accessing information, but teachers do much more than pass on facts. They motivate students, notice when someone is struggling and give emotional support. I think technology will change the teacher’s role rather than replace it.

p3.q: Is it better to learn in a classroom or online?
p3.model: It depends on the learner. Online learning is flexible and convenient, which suits adults with jobs. But for most young people, I think a classroom is better, because they need structure and the chance to interact with classmates. Many students find it hard to stay focused when they’re studying alone at home.

card.title: Describe a place you visited that you would like to go back to.
card.explain: and explain why you would like to go back.

items.model:
The place I’d like to talk about is AlUla, in the north-west of Saudi Arabia. I went there with my family about two years ago, during the winter holiday, and it was honestly one of the most memorable trips I’ve ever taken.

AlUla is famous for its dramatic landscape. There are huge sandstone mountains and rock formations in all kinds of strange shapes. One of the most well-known is Elephant Rock, which really does look like an elephant. We also visited the ancient tombs carved into the rocks, which are thousands of years old. Standing in front of them, I felt quite small; it’s amazing to think of the people who made them so long ago.

We stayed for three days. During the day we went on tours and took hundreds of photos, and in the evenings we ate at a restaurant in the old town, which has been restored with traditional mud-brick buildings. But the highlight for me was the night we spent at a desert camp. There was no light pollution at all, so the sky was completely full of stars. I’d never seen anything like it.

The reason I’d like to go back is that three days just wasn’t enough. There are hiking trails we didn’t have time for, and I’d love to try the hot-air balloon ride over the valley. Also, I was with my parents and younger brothers last time, so I’d like to go back with my friends and explore at a slower pace.

p3.q: Why do people like to visit historical places?
p3.model: I think many people are curious about how people lived in the past. Visiting historical sites makes history feel real in a way that books can’t. For some people, it’s also about identity, because seeing their own country’s heritage makes them feel proud and connected to their roots.

p3.q: How can tourism affect historical sites?
p3.model: It can have both positive and negative effects. On the positive side, money from tourism can pay for restoration and protection. On the other hand, large numbers of visitors can damage fragile sites, for example by touching walls or leaving rubbish. That’s why it’s important to limit visitor numbers in sensitive areas.

p3.q: Should historical sites be free to visit?
p3.model: In my opinion, there should be a charge, but it should be reasonable. The money is needed to maintain the sites. However, I think there should be discounts or free days for students and local residents, so that everyone has the chance to learn about their history.

card.title: Describe something you own that is very important to you.
card.explain: and explain why it is important to you.

items.model:
I’m going to talk about a watch that my grandfather gave me. It’s a fairly simple silver watch with a brown leather strap, nothing particularly expensive, but it means more to me than anything else I own.

My grandfather gave it to me on the day I graduated from secondary school. He had worn it himself for more than thirty years, and I remember he took it off his wrist in front of the whole family and put it on mine. He said something like, “Time is the one thing you can never get back, so use it well.” Everyone went quiet, and I was quite emotional.

I wear it almost every day, especially when I have something important, like an exam or an interview. I’ve had to replace the strap twice, and once the watch stopped working and I was really worried, but a watchmaker managed to repair it.

The reason it’s so important to me is partly because of my grandfather. He passed away last year, so the watch is a way of feeling that he’s still with me. But it’s also because of what he said. Whenever I’m wasting time, scrolling on my phone for example, I glance at the watch and remember his words, and it reminds me to get back to work. So in a way it’s not just a watch; it’s a kind of reminder of the person I want to be.

p3.q: Why do people keep things that have no practical use?
p3.model: Mainly because of memories. Objects can remind us of important people or moments in our lives, like a gift from someone we love or a souvenir from a special trip. They have emotional value, even if they’re not useful or expensive.

p3.q: Do young people today value possessions less than in the past?
p3.model: In some ways, yes. Young people tend to replace things quickly, especially phones and clothes, because new products appear all the time. On the other hand, many young people now prefer spending money on experiences, like travel, rather than on objects, which I think is quite positive.

p3.q: Is advertising making people more materialistic?
p3.model: I think it does play a role. Advertising often suggests that buying a product will make you happier or more successful, and social media makes this even stronger, because people constantly see what others own. But ultimately, it’s up to individuals and families to decide what really matters.

card.title: Describe a time when you had to solve a difficult problem.
card.explain: and explain how you felt about it.

items.model:
I’d like to describe a problem I faced last year during a group project at university. We were a team of four, and we had to design a small mobile app and present it to our professors at the end of the semester.

About three weeks before the deadline, one of our team members suddenly left the course for personal reasons. Unfortunately, he had been responsible for the whole back-end of the app, and when we checked his files, we discovered that most of the work hadn’t actually been done. So we had a huge amount of work and very little time.

At first, everyone panicked a bit, and there were some arguments about whose fault it was. But I suggested that we stop discussing the past and focus on what we could realistically finish. We made a list of all the features, removed the ones that weren’t essential, and divided the rest between the three of us according to our strengths. We also agreed to meet every evening for half an hour to check our progress. I spent a lot of late nights learning things I’d never done before, mostly from online tutorials.

In the end, we finished the app two days before the presentation, and it worked well. We got a good grade, although not the top one. I felt exhausted, but also really proud, because we didn’t give up. I think it taught me that when something goes wrong, staying calm and making a clear plan is much more useful than blaming people.

p3.q: Is it better to solve problems alone or in a group?
p3.model: It depends on the problem. Simple problems are often quicker to solve alone. But for complex problems, a group usually works better, because people bring different skills and ideas. The challenge is that groups need good communication, otherwise they can waste time arguing.

p3.q: What skills do children need to learn to solve problems?
p3.model: I think they need to learn to think critically and not give up easily. Schools could help by giving children open-ended tasks with more than one possible answer, instead of just memorising facts. Children also need to learn that making mistakes is a normal part of finding a solution.

p3.q: Do you think people rely too much on the internet to solve problems?
p3.model: To some extent, yes. Whenever we have a problem, our first reaction is to search online, which is useful but means we sometimes don’t think for ourselves. However, the internet also gives people access to expert knowledge they couldn’t get before, so overall I think it’s more helpful than harmful.

card.title: Describe a skill you would like to learn.
card.explain: and explain why you would like to learn it.

items.model:
A skill I’d really like to learn is photography. I don’t mean just taking photos on my phone, which everyone does, but properly understanding how to take professional-quality pictures.

I think I’d start with an online course, because there are some excellent ones that teach the basics, like how to use light and how to compose a picture. After that, I’d buy a second-hand camera, since new ones are very expensive, and practise as much as possible. There’s also a photography club in my city that organises trips to the desert and the old town, so I’d join that to learn from more experienced people.

I imagine it would be quite difficult at first. There are lots of technical things to understand, such as shutter speed and aperture, and I know that it takes years to develop a good eye. But I think the challenge is part of the fun.

The main reason I’d like to learn it is that I love travelling, and when I look back at my photos from previous trips, they never really capture what I saw. I’d like to be able to record those moments properly. Also, photography is becoming a valuable skill for many jobs, especially in marketing and social media, so it might even help my career. And finally, I think it would make me notice the world around me more carefully, which sounds like a good thing.

p3.q: What skills are most important for young people today?
p3.model: I’d say digital skills and communication skills are the most important. Almost every job now involves technology, so young people need to be comfortable with it. At the same time, being able to work in a team and express ideas clearly is just as important, and these are things machines can’t do as well.

p3.q: Is it easier to learn new skills as a child or as an adult?
p3.model: Children usually learn certain skills faster, especially languages and music. But adults have advantages too. They’re often more motivated, because they choose what they want to learn, and they can organise their learning better. So I think adults can learn very effectively if they’re committed.

p3.q: Should schools teach practical life skills?
p3.model: Definitely. Many young people leave school without knowing how to manage money, cook a basic meal or deal with official paperwork. Teaching these skills would make the transition to adult life much easier, and I don’t think it would take much time away from academic subjects.

card.title: Describe a celebration you enjoyed.
points: where and when it took place
card.explain: and explain why you enjoyed it.

items.model:
I’d like to talk about Eid al-Fitr last year, which we celebrated at my grandparents’ house in Abha. Eid always feels special, but last year was particularly memorable because, for the first time in several years, the whole extended family was together.

We arrived the night before, and the house was already full of activity. My aunts were preparing food, and my younger cousins were running around excitedly. On the morning of Eid, everyone woke up early, put on new clothes and went to the Eid prayer. Afterwards, we came back to my grandparents’ house for a huge breakfast with all kinds of traditional dishes and sweets.

There must have been around forty people there: my grandparents, my parents, my uncles and aunts, and lots of cousins, some of whom I hadn’t seen for years because they live abroad. The children received money and gifts from the adults, which is a tradition they always look forward to. In the afternoon, we visited neighbours and family friends, and in the evening there were fireworks in the city.

I think I enjoyed it so much because of the feeling of togetherness. These days everyone is so busy with work and studies, and families are spread across different cities and even countries. So having everyone in one place, sharing food and stories, made me realise how lucky I am to have such a close family. My grandparents were so happy that day, and that made it even more special for me.

p3.q: Why are celebrations important in a society?
p3.model: They bring people together and strengthen relationships, both within families and in the wider community. Celebrations also help to pass traditions and values from one generation to the next, so they’re an important part of a society’s identity.

p3.q: Have celebrations changed in recent years?
p3.model: Yes, I think they’ve become more commercial. People spend much more money on decorations, gifts and parties than in the past, and social media puts pressure on people to make everything look perfect. But the core of the celebrations, like visiting family, has stayed the same.

p3.q: Do you think big celebrations are a waste of money?
p3.model: Not necessarily. If people can afford them, they can create wonderful memories. The problem is when families feel they have to spend more than they can afford just to impress others. I think the most meaningful celebrations are often the simple ones.
